builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Do Coding Agents Follow AGENTS.md? The Effect of Policy Wording on Instruction Compliance
summary: The technique replaces unexamined or default policy wording in AGENTS.md-style context files with deliberately chosen phrasing styles, such as Prescriptive or Explanatory, to improve instruction compliance. It costs only authoring and prompt-maintenance effort, with negligible infrastructure overhead, but requires per-setup validation because the best wording was not stable across harness-model combinations. It can fail if a team standardizes on one style that performs worse for their specific agent stack or if improved wording still does not yield reliable policy adherence on real tasks.
rationale: This is directly relevant to production coding agents on constrained infrastructure, but the paper shows wording effects are setup-dependent, so teams should validate locally before standardizing.
technique: Policy wording optimization for agent context files

claims.statement: The technique replaces unexamined or default policy wording in AGENTS.md-style context files with deliberately chosen phrasing styles, such as Prescriptive or Explanatory, to improve instruction compliance. It costs only authoring and prompt-maintenance effort, with negligible infrastructure overhead, but requires per-setup validation because the best wording was not stable across harness-model combinations. It can fail if a team standardizes on one style that performs worse for their specific agent stack or if improved wording still does not yield reliable policy adherence on real tasks.
Conditional phrasing in Agent Context Files was followed less often than Prescriptive and Explanatory phrasing; the better of those two varied by harness-model combination.
